content: One study conducted in the United States explored midwives' perspectives and experiences regarding home births that occur on the periphery of healthcare organizations or facilities, within the broader healthcare system. This study emphasized the benefits of home birth settings, such as the absence of restrictions on women's movements, greater environmental comfort, and the lack of time constraints typically observed in institutional settings. In contrast, other studies included in the review highlighted significant challenges in institutional settings. These challenges included insufficient time, space, and facilities necessary for labor and normal birth. Additionally, access to operating theaters often influenced clinical decision-making. For example, hospital beds were sometimes moved back into labor rooms, and resources for non-pharmacological pain relief methods were not prioritized. Common barriers included inadequate space, insufficient staffing, the absence of bathtubs, limited availability of midwifery care for some women, and restrictive nutrition policies. In middle-income countries (MICs), concerns were raised about shared delivery rooms, which limited the presence of partners, family members, or other labor support companions. These rooms often lacked adequate facilities, such as proper lighting, toilets, showers, baths, or air conditioning. In some cases, delivery rooms were converted into operating theaters to accommodate the increasing number of cesarean sections (CSs). The methodological quality of the studies was generally robust, with 13 out of 16 studies reporting no or minor concerns regarding methodological limitations. Three studies had moderate concerns. Data coherence was high, with consistent findings across studies. The adequacy of data was also strong, with comprehensive information collected from five geographical regions, including high-income countries (HICs), MICs, and low-income countries (LICs). The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations for non-clinical interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. These recommendations are supported by evidence from various studies, which have been summarized in CERQual evidence tables. The studies reviewed include diverse perspectives on midwifery care, out-of-hospital birth settings, and strategies to promote normal birth practices while reducing cesarean section rates.
